# The Part I Can’t Leave in One Paragraph

Jess texted me last night: *It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.*

She wasn’t the only one in the group chat who thought I should let this go. I understand why. I’m not mad at her, and I’m not looking for a fight with the parent who complained. I just don’t think I can drop the project without explaining why—not in fifteen texts, anyway.

I teach two sections of US History II to juniors at Cobb Street High. For the past four years, one of their projects has been to interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston’s 1974–76 busing and desegregation crisis. They make a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. Until now, no one has complained.

This year, a parent emailed my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and copied a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” On Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, she, Dr. Halvorsen, and I will meet.

I think she has a point about pressure. Asking a teenager to interview a relative about a painful and complicated past can put them in a difficult position. A kid shouldn’t have to ask their grandmother to revisit something she’d rather not talk about—or feel they have to condemn a family member to write the reflection their teacher wants.

So I’m going to keep the project, but change it. Students who don’t want to interview someone in their family can speak with a librarian or archivist instead, or work with recorded interviews from previous years, with permission. No one has to interview a relative. That’s the line for me: kids who feel uncomfortable may have a lot to learn from the project, but I don’t get to force anyone into a conversation they don’t want to have.

I can see how that sounds like a compromise designed to keep the assignment alive. Maybe it is, partly. But I don’t think keeping it is the same as insisting every student participate in the same way.

The reason I care is that this is the history of the city these kids live in. Their textbook gives it one paragraph. They deserve more than that—not because I want them to arrive at a particular judgment about their families, but because the story is bigger and more human than a paragraph can hold.

In 2023, a student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. She’d never told anyone in the family. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class. Then nobody said a word for nearly a minute.

I don’t know what D. or his grandmother took away from that moment. I do know that the silence wasn’t empty. It was the kind you get when people are trying to understand something real before they decide what to say.

Last year, one student learned through her interview that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year—not because she reached the right conclusion, or because she turned her family into a tidy lesson, but because she sat with a hard discovery and tried to think carefully about it.

That’s not an argument that every kid should have to do the same thing. It’s an argument for making room for them to encounter history as something people lived, remembered, avoided, and sometimes only talked about years later.

Jess and I met student teaching at the same school in 2012. She left teaching in 2019 and now works in HR at a biotech in Cambridge. She knows what it is to care about a job and what it costs when the job stops fitting. I know she’s not warning me because she doesn’t care. She’s warning me because she does.

And she’s not wrong that I could get burned. I’m tenured—I have been since 2021—but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP. I’m not so secure that none of this matters. I’m honestly a little scared. I’m not feeling especially brave about it.

I’m also not choosing this because I want a public fight with a parent. I don’t. I think her concern about pressure is worth taking seriously, and I’m building that into the assignment. I just don’t want the answer to a difficult project to be that we stop asking students to learn about a difficult part of their own city.

So, Jess: I’m not asking you to agree with me, and I don’t think you need to change your mind. I just wanted you to know why I can’t quietly drop it. I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting—probably with the very uncinematic update that everyone was polite and we all went back to our day. Maybe we can talk then. Love you.
